lead: Cloud computing rents computing as a metered utility. A provider owns the machines and the network, and you buy capacity by the hour or by the request. The service model you choose fixes where your responsibility stops: the provider manages the layers below that line. The deployment model fixes who shares the hardware and who owns it. Together they explain most cloud bills, most cloud outages and most cloud lock-in. A Pune startup, a bank and a government office can all use the same provider under different models.
prereq: You need: Unit 4 for the characteristics and design challenges of distributed systems, and 6.1 for why remote storage must look local.

sections.h3: What counts as cloud: five tests

blocks.text: Cloud computing is a model for on-demand network access to a shared pool of computing resources — servers, storage, networks, applications — that can be provisioned and released quickly with little management effort. The provider owns the hardware; you rent capacity. Five tests separate a cloud from a plain data centre.

items: On-demand self-service: you create a VM or a database from a portal or API without asking a person.
Broad network access: services are reachable over the network from phones, laptops and office systems.
Resource pooling: many customers share a pool of machines, and the provider assigns and reassigns capacity.
Rapid elasticity: capacity grows or shrinks with demand, often in minutes.
Measured service: the provider meters use — hours, requests, gigabytes — and bills against the meter.

blocks.text: A data centre you own is not automatically a private cloud. It must pass these tests too.

sections.h3: Service models: who manages the stack

blocks.text: The service model sets the line between your work and the provider's work. The same application can be built at three levels.

IaaS (infrastructure as a service): you rent virtual machines, storage and networks. You install and patch the operating system, the runtime and the application. Amazon EC2 and Azure Virtual Machines are examples.

PaaS (platform as a service): the provider runs the servers and the operating system. You deploy code and data; the provider patches the runtime and scales the workers. Google App Engine and Heroku are examples.
SaaS (software as a service): the provider runs everything. You open a browser and use the application. Gmail and Salesforce are examples.

Two newer labels split the same stack differently. Serverless, or function as a service, runs a function per event and bills per invocation and execution time; you do not manage a server. Database as a service gives you a managed database with backups and patching done for you.
The line is not fixed. A managed Kubernetes service is closer to PaaS than to raw IaaS. In every case, ask who patches the OS and who owns the data.
The deployment model says who owns the hardware and who shares it.

items: Public cloud: a provider owns the hardware and many customers share it. Tenants are isolated by software.
Private cloud: one organisation uses the cloud, on its own hardware or hosted. It still needs self-service, pooling and metering.
Community cloud: several organisations with a shared concern — a group of banks, a set of hospitals — share a cloud.
Hybrid cloud: two or more models are joined so data and applications can move between them.

blocks.text: Cloud turns capital cost into operating cost. A team avoids buying servers and pays monthly. Provisioning takes minutes, not weeks. A service can reach users in many regions, and capacity can stretch for exam-week peaks, then shrink.

The risks are real. Vendor lock-in grows when you use proprietary APIs. Data security and privacy remain your duty even when the provider secures the hardware. Compliance and data residency may require data to stay in a country. Downtime, latency, network dependence and surprise bills follow from renting someone else's machines.
AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud are the largest public platforms; Oracle Cloud and IBM Cloud also serve enterprises. India's MeghRaj is a government cloud initiative for public departments.

figure.caption: The stack shows where your work begins. The top layer is a finished application; the lower layer leaves the operating system and runtime to you.

spec.aria: A three-layer stack of cloud service models, from SaaS at the top where the user only consumes the application, down to IaaS where the user manages the operating system and everything above it.

examples.question: A startup in Pune runs an exam-practice app. Option 1 is IaaS: one VM of 2 vCPU and 4 GB at ₹2.5 per hour, running 24×7. Option 2 is PaaS: ₹1,500 base per month plus ₹0.9 per 1,000 requests, with 3 million requests per month. Use 730 hours in a month. Compare the monthly bills.
steps: IaaS hours in a month = 730 hours.
IaaS bill = 730 hours × ₹2.5 per hour = ₹1,825 per month.
PaaS request blocks = 3,000,000 requests ÷ 1,000 requests per block = 3,000 blocks.
PaaS request charge = 3,000 blocks × ₹0.9 per block = ₹2,700.
IaaS is cheaper in money by ₹2,375 per month, but the team must patch the OS and runtime itself.
examples.answer: IaaS costs ₹1,825 per month and PaaS costs ₹4,200 per month; IaaS is cheaper by ₹2,375, but PaaS includes OS patching.
examples.check:
hours = 730
iaas_rate = 2.5
iaas_cost = hours * iaas_rate
requests = 3_000_000
base = 1500
per_thousand = 0.9
paas_cost = base + (requests / 1000) * per_thousand
print(iaas_cost)
print(paas_cost)
print(paas_cost - iaas_cost)

traps: Calling any owned data centre a private cloud. A private cloud still needs self-service, resource pooling, elasticity and measured service; without them it is just virtualised servers.
Mixing PaaS with SaaS. PaaS gives you a runtime to deploy your own code; SaaS gives you a finished application that you only use.
Assuming IaaS is always cheaper. The VM bill is lower, but OS patching, backups and staff time are now your cost.
Ignoring data residency. A public cloud region outside your country may break a compliance rule even when the technology works.
Treating elasticity as infinite. Quotas, budgets and database limits can stop scaling.

quiz.q: List the five essential characteristics of cloud computing.
quiz.a: On-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity and measured service.

quiz.q: Why is an organisation's own data centre not automatically a private cloud?
quiz.a: A private cloud still needs self-service, pooling, elasticity and metering. Without those it is only virtualised servers.

quiz.q: State the difference between PaaS and SaaS.
quiz.a: PaaS gives a runtime; you deploy your code. SaaS gives a finished application; you only use it.

quiz.q: A VM costs ₹3 per hour and runs 730 hours a month. A PaaS plan costs ₹2,000 a month plus ₹1 per 1,000 requests, with 5,000,000 requests. Compute both bills and say which is cheaper.
A firm uses a public cloud for a customer app and a private cloud for payroll data. Name the deployment model and give one benefit and one risk.
quiz.a: Hybrid cloud. Benefit: the app can burst and reach users globally while payroll stays controlled. Risk: data movement and two security policies are harder to govern.

quiz.q: Classify each as SaaS, PaaS or IaaS: (a) Gmail, (b) a rented VM where you install Linux, (c) a service where you upload Python code and the provider patches the OS.
Cloud reduces capital cost but can raise operating cost. Explain this shift and give one control that keeps the bill predictable.
quiz.a: Buying servers is capital cost; cloud use is a monthly operating cost billed by meter. Demand can grow without a purchase decision, so bills surprise. Controls: budgets, quotas, tagging, auto-scaling limits and reserved capacity.

beyond: Not for the exam. Cloud-native work now builds on containers and orchestration, service meshes and observability, and the exam-level models sit underneath those tools. Cost control has its own name, FinOps, and data residency is a live legal topic in many countries. Useful search terms: serverless cold start, confidential computing and cloud egress charges.
